name: Food that keeps
desc: Preserving in jars, jam, freezing, a food store, dried meat, hard bread, smoking fish, and how to tell if food is still safe

guides.t: How to make food keep: the basics
guides.w: Read this before you preserve anything
s: Food goes off because of germs, moulds and yeasts. They need water, warmth, air and time. Every way of preserving takes one of those away.
Take away water: drying (fruit, herbs, mushrooms, meat).
Make it too salty, too sweet or too sour for germs: salting, jam, pickling in vinegar, fermenting.
Heat it and seal it: jars in a boiling water bath. Only for sour food like fruit, jam and pickles.
Keep it cold: fridge (4 °C or less) and freezer (−18 °C).
Work clean: wash your hands, boards, knives and jars in hot soapy water first.
Write the contents and the date on every jar or bag, and eat the oldest first.
d: Never preserve vegetables, beans, meat or fish in a water bath or in oil at room temperature: that's how botulism happens
When in doubt, throw it out
guides.src: Voedingscentrum / USDA National Center for Home Food Preservation

guides.w: Fruit, jam, pickles and tomatoes that keep for a year
s: Only for sour (acidic) food: fruit, jam, chutney, vegetables pickled in vinegar, and tomatoes with lemon juice added (1 tablespoon per half-litre jar).
Use jars without chips and new lids, or Weck jars with fresh rubber rings. Wash them in hot soapy water and keep them hot.
Fill the jars with the hot food, leaving 1 cm free at the top (0.5 cm for jam). Wipe the rim clean and close the lids.
Put the jars on a cloth or rack in a big pan and add water until it covers the lids by 2–3 cm.
Bring it to a rolling boil, then start the clock: about 10 minutes for jam, 15–20 for fruit, 35–45 for tomatoes. Keep it boiling.
Lift the jars out and let them cool for 24 hours without touching them.
Check the seal: the lid is pulled down and doesn't click, or the Weck lid holds when you remove the clips. Not sealed? Keep it in the fridge and eat it this week.
Store sealed jars cool and dark, and use them within a year.
d: No water bath for vegetables, beans, meat or fish: they need a pressure canner
Don't eat from a jar with a bulging lid, foam, a bad smell or liquid spurting out
guides.src: USDA National Center for Home Food Preservation

s: Use ripe fruit without bruises. Wash it, remove stones and stalks, and cut it small.
Classic jam: equal weights of fruit and sugar (1 kg fruit, 1 kg sugar). With jam sugar (geleisuiker) follow the packet: it has pectin, so it sets faster and needs less sugar.
Heat the fruit and sugar slowly until the sugar has dissolved, then boil it hard while stirring. With jam sugar about 4 minutes; with plain sugar longer.
Set test: put a spoonful on a cold saucer. If it wrinkles when you push it after a minute, it's ready.
Pour it hot into hot, clean jars up to 0.5 cm from the top and close them straight away.
For a year on the shelf: give the jars 10 minutes in a boiling water bath (see Preserving in jars).
Low-sugar jam doesn't keep like real jam: keep it in the fridge and eat it within a few weeks.
d: Mould on jam: throw the whole jar away, don't just scrape it off
guides.src: Voedingscentrum / USDA National Center for Home Food Preservation

guides.w: The easiest way to keep almost anything
s: Your freezer should be −18 °C or colder. A cheap freezer thermometer tells you.
Most vegetables keep better if you blanch them first: boil for 1–3 minutes (peas 1½, carrots 2, beans and broccoli 3), then straight into ice-cold water for the same time.
Dry them well and freeze them spread out on a tray first, so they don't stick together. Then put them in bags.
Press all the air out of the bags, or use boxes filled to the top: air causes freezer burn (dry grey patches).
Freeze in portions you'll use at once, flat so they freeze and thaw fast. Write the contents and date on them.
Roughly how long: vegetables and fruit 8–12 months, raw meat 6–12, mince 3–4, fatty fish 2–3, bread and leftovers 2–3 months.
Thaw meat and fish in the fridge, not on the counter. Thawed raw food can go back in the freezer only after you've cooked it.
d: Don't put warm food straight in the freezer: let it cool first, but within 2 hours
Don't refreeze raw meat or fish that has thawed

guides.w: A cupboard that gets you through two weeks
s: Start with 3 days (the government advice), then build up to two weeks for everyone in the house.

Choose food that keeps for a year or more and that you eat anyway: rice, pasta, oats, lentils and dried beans, tins of fish, beans, vegetables and fruit, crackers, peanut butter, honey, UHT milk, oil, salt and sugar.
Add food you can eat without cooking, for when there is no power: tins, crackers, nuts, dried fruit, muesli bars.
Keep it cool, dark and dry, in closed boxes or jars against damp, mice and moths.
First in, first out: put new shopping at the back and take from the front, so nothing gets old.
Check twice a year (for example when the clocks change) and use up what's getting near its date.
Don't forget a hand tin opener, water (3 litres per person per day), and food for babies, pets and special diets.
d: Don't buy food nobody in the house likes: you won't rotate it and it will go to waste

guides.t: Is it still safe to eat?
guides.w: Dates, smells, mould and dented tins
s: ‘Te gebruiken tot’ / ‘use by’: eat it by that date. After it, throw it away, even if it looks fine (meat, fish, fresh dairy).
‘Ten minste houdbaar tot’ / ‘best before’: about quality, not safety. Often fine for a long time after: look, smell and taste a little.
Tins: throw them away if they bulge, leak, spurt when opened, are badly rusted or have a deep dent on the seam.
Jars: a lid that has come loose or bulges, foam, cloudy liquid or a strange smell means throw it out.
Mould on bread, jam, soft cheese, yoghurt or leftovers: throw the whole thing away. Hard cheese: cut away at least 2 cm around the mould.
After a power cut: if the fridge was above 7 °C for more than 4 hours, throw away meat, fish, eggs, dairy and leftovers. Frozen food that still has ice crystals may go back in the freezer.
d: Don't taste food you're unsure about: some dangerous germs have no smell or taste
Never eat from a bulging tin, not even a little

guides.t: Garlic and herbs in oil: the hidden danger
guides.w: It looks lovely in the jar
s: Garlic, fresh herbs, chilli or vegetables in oil can grow botulism germs: no air, not sour, room temperature. You can't see, smell or taste it.
Making flavoured oil for now: keep it in the fridge and use it within 4 days.
For longer: freeze it, for example chopped herbs or garlic in oil in an ice-cube tray.
Dried herbs or dried tomatoes in oil are much safer, but still keep them in the fridge.
Shop-bought jars are made safe with acid and heat. Once opened, keep them in the fridge.
d: Never keep garlic or fresh herbs in oil at room temperature

guides.w: Catch of the day, keeps a few extra days
s: Clean the fish and leave the skin on. Fatty fish works best: mackerel, herring, trout, salmon.
Put it in brine for 1–2 hours: about 80 grams of salt per litre of water, in the fridge.
Rinse it, pat it dry and let it dry in the air for an hour until the surface feels tacky.
Smoke it hot, at 70–90 °C, with wood chips (beech, oak, alder or fruit wood, no resinous wood) in a smoker, a kettle barbecue with a lid or a closed tin box over embers.
It's done when the flesh is cooked right through and flakes: at least 63 °C in the thickest part. Usually 1–2 hours.
Let it cool and keep it in the fridge: eat it within 3–4 days, or freeze it.
d: Don't cold-smoke at home without real knowledge: it doesn't cook the fish and can make you ill
Never smoke indoors or in a closed garage

s: Use lean beef or game. Trim off all fat (fat goes rancid) and freeze it for an hour so it's easy to slice.
Cut it into strips about 5 mm thick, across the grain for tender jerky.
Marinate for a few hours in the fridge: salt or soy sauce with spices.
Make it safe: first heat the strips in the marinade until they reach 71 °C, or bake the dried strips for 10 minutes at 135 °C afterwards.
Dry the strips on a rack in an oven at 60–70 °C with the door open a crack, or in a food dryer, for 4–8 hours.
Ready when it bends and cracks but doesn't break. Keep it in a closed jar for 1–2 months, longer in the fridge or freezer.
d: Don't skip the heating step: drying alone doesn't kill all germs in meat
guides.src: USDA Food Safety and Inspection Service

guides.t: Hard bread that keeps for months
s: Mix 500 g flour, 1 teaspoon of salt and about 200 ml water into a stiff dough that doesn't stick.
Roll it out 1 cm thick and cut it into squares of about 8 by 8 cm.
Prick holes all over both sides with a fork or skewer, so it dries right through.
Bake for 30 minutes at 190 °C, turn them over and bake 30 minutes more.
Let them dry out completely for a day or two on a rack: they should be rock hard.
Kept dry in a closed tin they last for months. Soak a piece in soup, coffee or water before eating, or fry it.
d: Moisture spoils them: no plastic bags while they're still warm
